label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
# My van almost caught fire last week. Here's what went wrong, and what to check on yours.

This isn't a fun one, sorry. I've started writing it about four times and kept closing the laptop. But Tasha is about to put a deposit down on a build, and I know a bunch of you who read this are running mobile setups or saving up for one. So I'm going to write it all down properly while it's fresh.

First, so nobody panics: **everyone is fine.** Me, the dog, the client, all fine. The van is not fine, and I'm off the road for at least a few weeks. But nobody got hurt.

Second, and I'll say this a few more times: **I am not an electrician.** I'm a dog groomer. Everything technical in here is what a real electrician explained to me while I stood in her shop nodding and trying not to cry. I've tried really hard to get the numbers right, but please don't treat this post as electrical advice. Treat it as "here's what happened to someone like you, and here's what made me go get a pro to look." Then go get a pro to look.

---

## What happened

Wednesday, October 28, around 2:15 in the afternoon. I was parked in a client's driveway in Bedford drying Moose. Moose is a Bernese, so if you've ever dried a Bernese you know this is not a five-minute job. The dryer was on high and had been for a while.

I started smelling hot plastic. I figured it was the dryer motor working hard, because honestly that thing smells a bit on a big double coat anyway, and I kept going. That's the part I keep replaying. I kept going.

A minute or two later I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat. That's where my batteries live.

I don't totally remember deciding what to do, I just did it. I killed the battery switch, got Moose out the side door (still damp and absolutely delighted about it, he thought it was a game), and then went back with the extinguisher. I gave it a short blast. I'm honestly not sure I needed to. I think killing the switch had mostly done it. But I wasn't going to stand there and find out.

When I could actually look, the lug on the end of the positive cable was black, and the cable jacket had melted back about 3 cm from the end.

Moose's mom came out, saw what was going on, went back inside and came back with a coffee for me. Then she just sat with me on her front steps while I shook. I'm not going to name her because she'd hate it, but if you're reading this, thank you. I will never forget that.

---

## My setup (so you can compare to yours)

Here's what I had, because I think this is the useful part for anyone with a similar build:

- **Inverter:** 3000W
- **Batteries:** two 200Ah lithium, 12V system
- **Built by:** Coastline Van Fitouts (Darren), spring 2025
- **What I run off it:** the dryer, which pulls roughly 1800 to 2000W, and sometimes the water heater on top of that

It looked great. The wiring was tidy, everything was neatly zip-tied, all the ends had nice heat-shrink on them. I trusted it because it looked so clean.

**Tidy is not the same as right.** That's probably the main thing I want you to take from this whole post.

---

## What the electrician found

I took the van to Priya at Sackville Marine Electric. She was amazing. Patient, didn't make me feel stupid, explained everything twice. Here's what she showed me, in the plainest words I can manage.

### 1. The main cable was way too small

The cable running from my battery to my inverter was **4 AWG**. Priya says for a 3000W inverter on a 12V system it should have been **2/0**.

If you're like me and AWG means nothing to you: it's a wire size, and the numbers go *backwards*. A smaller number means a thicker wire. 2/0 (said "two-aught") is a lot thicker than 4. Like, noticeably. She held a piece of each up next to each other and I actually said "oh no" out loud.

Here's the math as she explained it to me. On a 12V system, amps are roughly watts divided by volts:

- Dryer alone at 1800 to 2000W ÷ 12V = roughly **150 to 165 amps**
- Add the water heater and you're up around **200 to 250 amps**
- The inverter itself isn't 100% efficient, and battery voltage drops a bit under heavy load, so the real number pulled from the battery is a bit higher than the simple math says

That's a lot of current going through one cable, and a 4 AWG cable isn't meant to carry that kind of load continuously. And drying a Bernese is about as continuous as it gets. A cable that's too small for what's going through it heats up. That's basically the whole story.

### 2. The crimp on the lug was bad

A lug is the metal ring on the end of the cable that bolts onto the battery or the inverter. It's supposed to be squished onto the wire with a proper crimping tool (a big heavy-duty one, often hydraulic, for cables this size) so the metal is pressed tight all the way around.

Mine wasn't. Priya cut the heat-shrink off and you could see it had been squeezed with something like pliers or a hammer. It was kind of mashed in one spot instead of crimped evenly. The heat-shrink had been covering it up, which is why it looked so neat from the outside.

A bad crimp means a bad connection, and a bad connection gets hot. Put a bad connection on a cable that's already too small and already working hard, and that's where it melted. Right at the lug, on the positive end.

### 3. The fuse was too far from the battery

There *was* a fuse. It was a 300A ANL fuse. But it was mounted about **90 cm** from the battery. Priya said it should be within about **18 cm** of the battery.

The way she explained it: the fuse only protects the cable that comes *after* it. Everything between the battery and the fuse is basically unprotected. So I had almost a metre of cable with nothing guarding it.

One more thing I learned while trying to understand all this, and please confirm it with your own electrician because I'm still wrapping my head around it: the fuse is supposed to be sized to protect the *wire*, not just the inverter. A 300A fuse on a 4 AWG cable means the cable can get dangerously hot long before the fuse ever blows. So even if my fuse had been in the right spot, I'm not sure it would have saved me here. Ask about this one. It's worth understanding.

### 4. No smoke detector in the back

The only smoke detector I had was the one in the cab that came with the van. Nothing in the back where the batteries and all the equipment are. I noticed the smell and the smoke because I was standing right there. If I'd stepped out to talk to a client, or if this had happened while the van was parked and charging, I wouldn't have known.

### The thermal camera thing

This is the part that really got me. Priya pulled up my damage photos on her screen, and next to them she put thermal camera shots of her own van running a similar kind of load. Hers barely gets warm. The cables and connections just look like normal, boring, room-temperature cables.

Same kind of job. Same kind of power. One of them melted and one of them barely notices. That difference is entirely down to how it was built. Seeing them side by side was wild.

---

## The repair

Priya's quote is **$4,200**. That covers:

- Rewiring the main runs with the right size cable
- A new fuse block
- A **Class T fuse**, which she says is the right kind for lithium batteries at this size
- Doing all the crimps properly

It's **three weeks minimum**, because parts are on order.

I've cancelled **31 appointments** so far. That number is going to go up.

Insurance says "maybe." The adjuster is coming Thursday. I'll update when I know more.

---

## About the builder

I want to be careful here. I'm not trying to trash anybody publicly. I'm just going to tell you the facts and you can make up your own mind.

My van was built by Darren at Coastline Van Fitouts in spring 2025. Since this happened I've sent him three texts and an email explaining what happened and what the electrician found. As of writing this, I haven't heard back.

That's it. That's all I'm going to say about it.

---

## Tasha, this part is for you (and anyone else about to pay a deposit)

Before you hand over any money to *any* builder, ask them to put these things **in writing**:

1. **What size cable will run from the battery to the inverter?** Get the actual AWG number. For a 3000W inverter on 12V, if they say something like 4 AWG, ask them to explain why. (Better yet, ask an electrician to check whatever number they give you.)
2. **What fuse are they using, what's the rating, and how far from the battery will it be mounted?** You want the type (like Class T or ANL), the amp rating, and the distance.
3. **Is the fuse sized to protect the cable?** Make them actually answer this one.
4. **What tool do they use to crimp the big cables?** You want to hear something like "a hydraulic crimper." You do not want to hear a vague answer.
5. **Will they give you a wiring diagram when it's done?** You should get one. It makes it so much easier for an electrician to check later.
6. **Will there be a smoke detector in the back near the batteries?** Ask for one if not.
7. **Can you get an independent electrician to inspect it before you pay the final balance?** A good builder shouldn't have a problem with this. If they get weird about it, that tells you something.

Also, tell them exactly what you'll be running. Say "a high-velocity dryer at about 2000W for long stretches, plus a water heater." Don't just say "a dryer." Long continuous loads are a different thing from running a coffee maker for three minutes, and the build needs to be designed around that.

I didn't ask any of this. I looked at nice tidy wiring and assumed it was fine. Please don't be me.

---

## A checklist you can do on your own van (with the power OFF)

This is stuff anyone can look at. You don't need to know anything about electrical to spot most of it. You just need to know what you're looking for.

**Before you start: turn everything off.** Kill your main battery disconnect switch. Turn off the inverter. Unplug from shore power if you're plugged in. Don't poke around live battery connections. Seriously, these batteries can put out a scary amount of current. This checklist is *looking*, not fixing.

**☐ Find your main cable and read it.**
Most cables have the size printed right on the jacket in tiny letters. Look for something like "4 AWG" or "2/0." Take a photo. If you've got a big inverter (2000W+) on a 12V system and the cable is something like 4 AWG, get an electrician to look at it.

**☐ Measure how far your main fuse is from the battery.**
Follow the positive cable from the battery terminal to the first fuse. Grab a tape measure. If it's way more than about 18 cm, flag it.

**☐ Check what fuse you have.**
Write down the type and the amp number printed on it. Take a photo. This is useful to bring to an electrician.

**☐ Look at every lug and connection you can see.**
You're looking for:
- Any discolouration: dark, brown, black, or rainbow-ish metal
- Heat-shrink that looks shrivelled, bubbled, shiny-melted, or pulled back
- Cable jacket that's hard, cracked, or melted near the end
- Lugs that look squashed or dented unevenly instead of smoothly pressed

**☐ Give the cables a gentle wiggle at the lugs (power off!).**
A proper crimp shouldn't move at all. If the cable shifts or twists inside the lug, that's a problem.

**☐ Feel the cable jacket near the ends.**
Does it feel brittle or stiff compared to the rest of the cable? That can mean it's been getting hot.

**☐ Check your smoke detector situation.**
Do you have one in the back, near the batteries and the equipment? If not, get one. They're cheap. I'd also think about a CO detector if you have anything fuel-burning in there.

**☐ Find your extinguisher and make sure you can grab it fast.**
Is it charged? Is it somewhere you can actually reach in a hurry, not buried under towels and shampoo jugs? Mine was reachable and I'm really glad.

**☐ Know where your battery disconnect is without thinking.**
Practise it. In the moment I didn't have to think, and that was huge.

**☐ Ask for (or find) your wiring diagram.**
If your builder never gave you one, that alone is worth asking about.

If anything on this list looks off, **don't try to fix it yourself.** Take photos and book an electrician. Ideally someone who does marine or RV/van electrical, because they deal with exactly this kind of 12V high-current stuff.

---

## Get a cheap infrared thermometer

Everyone should own one. I got mine for 40 bucks at Canadian Tire. It's a little gun-shaped thing you point at something and it tells you the temperature without touching it.

Here's how I'm going to use mine once the van is back:

- Run your normal load for a while. For me that's the dryer on high for a good chunk of time, like a real full dry.
- **Don't touch anything.** Just point the thermometer at your main cables, the lugs, the fuse, and the inverter connections from a safe distance.
- Compare. Connections should be pretty close to the temperature of the cable around them. If one spot is way hotter than everything else, that's your warning sign.
- Do it every so often, not just once. Things can loosen over time with all the driving and vibration.

It's not as good as a real thermal camera like Priya's, and it's not a replacement for an inspection. But it would have caught what was happening in my van, and I'd have caught it before anything melted.

And if you smell hot plastic: **stop.** Don't assume it's the dryer motor. Turn things off and check. I lost a minute or two thinking it was nothing, and I'm lucky that's all it cost.

---

## Where I'm at

Honestly? Not great. I'm scared. My whole income is that van. There's no backup, there's no other way for me to work right now. Rent is due on the 1st. I've cancelled 31 appointments and I'm going to cancel more. Insurance is a maybe. I keep doing math at 2am.

I also keep thinking about what would have happened if I'd been out of the van, or if Moose had been crated in there, or if it had been parked overnight on a charger. I try not to go too far down that road.

But I'm okay. Moose is okay. The van can be fixed, and it's going to be fixed *properly* this time. Priya has been great, and so many of you have reached out already. I've read every message even if I haven't answered yet.

To all my clients who've been so patient about cancellations: thank you. I'll be in touch the second I have a date.

Tasha, please ask the questions. Get it all in writing. I love you, I'm not trying to scare you off, I just really don't want this to happen to you.

And everyone else, go look at your cables this weekend. Power off, tape measure, phone camera. It takes 20 minutes.

I'll post again when the van's back. I'll show you what the new wiring looks like next to the old stuff, because I think seeing it side by side will help more than anything I can write here.

Talk soon. 🐾

*(One more time, because it matters: I'm not an electrician. This is just what happened to me and what I learned. If you're worried about your setup, please get a qualified electrician to inspect it.)*
